a: PCA maximises variance, and variance depends on units. A feature in rupees has huge variance and would dominate PC1 regardless of importance. Standardising means PCA works on correlations.

q: How many components do you keep?
a: Enough to explain a target share of variance (often 90–95%), the elbow of the scree plot, eigenvalue > 1 (Kaiser rule on standardised data), or the number that gives the best downstream CV score.

q: Can PCA hurt a supervised model?
a: Yes. PCA is unsupervised: it keeps high-variance directions, but the target might depend on a low-variance direction that gets dropped. Use PCA when you need compression or decorrelation, and verify with CV. PLS or LDA consider the target.

Partially: each is a weighted combination of all original features (loadings). You can describe PC1 by its largest loadings ("overall spend level"), but it's harder to explain than original features, a downside in regulated settings.

PCA: linear, fast, preserves global variance, can transform new data, usable as features. t-SNE: non-linear, preserves local neighbourhoods, for 2D visualisation only; cluster sizes and distances between clusters are not meaningful. UMAP: non-linear, faster, preserves more global structure, can transform new points.

Libraries use SVD of the centred data matrix \(X = USV^\top\). It's numerically more stable and avoids forming \(X^\top X\). The columns of V are the principal directions and \(s_k^2/(n-1)\) are the eigenvalues.
Yes: principal components are uncorrelated by construction, so regression on components (principal component regression) has no multicollinearity, at the cost of interpretability.
